message.content:
Below is a concise summary of your key rights and protections under Texas law when you’re renting a residential property. (This isn’t legal advice—if you have a specific dispute, consult an attorney or your local tenant‑rights organization.) | Area | What the law says | Practical take‑away | |------|-------------------|---------------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlords may charge up to **$1,000** for a single‑unit apartment or **$2,000** for a multi‑family dwelling.
• Must be returned within **30 days** after you move out, minus any lawful deductions. | Keep a written receipt and inventory list at move‑in; keep photos/notes of existing damage. | | **Move‑In Inspection** | Landlord must give you a written “move‑in” inspection report. | Request a copy before signing the lease; note any pre‑existing damages. | | **Habitability / Repairs** | • Landlord must maintain plumbing, heating, electrical, structural integrity, and pest control.
• If repairs aren’t made within a reasonable time, you may withhold rent or repair & deduct (but only if you follow proper procedure). | Document all repair requests in writing; send a certified mail notice if you need to withhold rent. | | **Notice Requirements** | • For month‑to‑month leases: 30‑day written notice to terminate.
• For fixed‑term leases: landlord must give you a written notice of intent to not renew at least **60 days** before the lease ends. | Keep copies of all notices; use certified mail or email with read receipts. | | **Rent Increases** | No statutory limit on how much a landlord can raise rent, but they must give **30 days’ written notice** for increases during a month‑to‑month tenancy. | Review your lease for any “rent increase clause”; if it’s missing, you’re protected by the 30‑day rule. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlord must serve a **10‑day notice** for nonpayment of rent.
• A **30‑day notice** for other breaches (e.g., violating lease terms).
• After the notice period, the landlord files an unlawful detainer action in court. | Do not ignore notices; respond promptly. If you receive a notice, you can file a counter‑claim or request a hearing. | | **Right to Quiet Enjoyment** | Landlord cannot enter without **reasonable notice** (usually 24 hours) except in emergencies. | Ask for a written entry log; if entries happen without notice, you can file a complaint. | | **Discrimination Protections** | Under federal Fair Housing Act and Texas Civil Rights Code, landlords cannot discriminate based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or source of income. | Report discrimination to the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) or Texas Attorney General. | | **Lease Modification** | Any changes to the lease must be in writing and signed by both parties. | Keep copies of all amendments. | | **Legal Remedies** | • You can sue for unpaid security deposits, damages, or breach of contract.
• You can seek a refund of overpaid rent or a court order to stop illegal evictions. | File claims in small‑claims court (up to $20,000) or civil court for larger amounts. | ### Where to Get Help | Resource | How it helps | |----------|--------------| | **Texas Attorney General – Consumer Protection Division** | Handles complaints against landlords, provides consumer guides. | | **Local Housing Authority / City Clerk’s Office** | Offers mediation services, local ordinances, and enforcement. | | **Texas Tenants Association** | Non‑profit advocacy group offering legal clinics and resources. | | **Small Claims Court** | Quick, low‑cost venue for disputes under $20,000. | | **Legal Aid Organizations** | Free or reduced‑fee representation for qualifying tenants. | --- #### Quick Checklist Before Signing a Lease 1. **Read the entire lease** – look for clauses on rent increases, maintenance responsibilities, and termination procedures. 2. **Ask for a written move‑in inspection** – get a copy signed by both parties. 3. **Confirm the security deposit amount** – ensure it doesn’t exceed the statutory limit. 4. **Verify the landlord’s contact info** – make sure you know how to reach them for emergencies. 5. **Keep records** – emails, texts, and certified mail receipts for all communications. If you encounter a situation where your landlord violates any of these rights, you can file a formal complaint with the Texas Attorney General or seek legal assistance from a local tenant‑rights organization.
